bib.title: How Much Knowledge Can You Pack Into the Parameters of a Language Model?

question: How much knowledge can a pre-trained language model store in its parameters, measured by fine-tuning it to answer open-domain questions with no external context (closed-book QA)?
hypothesis: Larger models store more knowledge, so closed-book QA performance should scale with model size and be competitive with open-book retrieval systems.
contributions: Define and evaluate closed-book QA with T5 up to 11B parameters
Show performance scales with size and that salient span masking pre-training gives a large boost
Human evaluation showing exact match underestimates closed-book accuracy

method.summary: Fine-tune pre-trained T5 (and T5.1.1) text-to-text models to output the answer from the question alone on NQ, WebQuestions and TriviaQA, optionally after 100,000 steps of extra salient span masking pre-training. Compared with open-book retrieve-and-read systems.

datasets.name: Natural Questions (open-domain)
datasets.split: 10% of train held out as validation, rest for fine-tuning; dev set reported
datasets.preprocessing: Questions only; first answer only; answers over five tokens dropped; unanswerable and long answers omitted

datasets.name: WebQuestions
datasets.split: 10% of train held out as validation; test reported

datasets.name: TriviaQA
datasets.split: 10% of train held out; dev reported, plus official test via leaderboard (Wikipedia domain, unfiltered training set)

datasets.name: Wikipedia sentence dataset with salient spans (Guu et al. 2020)
datasets.source: Guu et al. 2020, BERT-mined sentences with named entities and dates

models.name: T5 (Base, Large, 3B, 11B)
models.init_from: Raffel et al. 2019 checkpoints, pre-trained on C4 span corruption plus supervised multitask mixture

models.name: T5.1.1 (Base, Large, XL, XXL)
models.params: XXL described as comparably-sized to 11B; others not stated
models.init_from: T5.1.1 checkpoints, pre-trained on unlabeled data only

training.objective: maximum likelihood on literal answer text given question with task prefix; optional SSM continued pre-training
training.steps: 20,000 fine-tuning steps; 100,000 additional SSM pre-training steps
training.dropout: 10% (doubled for WebQuestions); 5% for all three datasets with T5.1.1

other.note: validation accuracy plateaued after a few hundred steps

inference.decoding: greedy (most likely token at each timestep)
inference.samples: inferred: one run per configuration, no seeds reported
inference.prompting: question with task-specific prefix as input, answer text as output

metrics.name: exact match
metrics.definition: prediction equals a ground-truth answer after lowercasing and stripping articles, punctuation, duplicate whitespace

metrics.name: recall (multi-answer NQ)
metrics.definition: correct only if all answers for any one annotator are predicted

eval.protocol: single run; 150 NQ validation misses hand-inspected by the authors for false negatives

limits: Largest models (about 11B) needed for state of the art; expensive in resource-constrained settings
No indication of which information was used; knowledge distributed inexplicably; model hallucinates realistic answers when unsure
Maximum likelihood gives no guarantee a fact is learned; cannot update or remove knowledge
Tasks measure trivia-style knowledge, not reasoning (DROP suggested)
Exact match underestimates accuracy; the 57.8 adjustment comes from a 150-example inspection by the authors
Dataset sizes, hardware, compute, seeds and tokenizer not stated
